title: Picky Eating Is Normal
hook: Picky eating is a normal toddler stage, not a battle to win. The reliable approach: you decide what and when to offer, your child decides whether and how much to eat.
key_points: Picky eating is a normal developmental stage as a toddler's growth — and appetite — naturally slows after infancy.
Division of responsibility: the parent provides the food and the setting; the child chooses whether and how much to eat.
Keep offering rejected foods calmly; it can take 10 or more tastes before a toddler accepts a new food.
Skip pressure, bribes, and short-order cooking — forcing foods can make a child dislike them more.
content_html: If your toddler suddenly eats almost nothing but crackers, take a breath — picky eating is a normal developmental stage. After the fast growth of infancy, a toddler's growth rate and appetite naturally slow, so smaller, choosier eating is common. The AAP's framing is reassuring: it's the parent's job to provide the food, and the child's decision to eat it.
extra_html: That "division of responsibility" is the key. You decide what's offered and when; your child decides whether and how much to eat from what's on the table. Keep serving the family meal without cooking separate dishes, and keep offering foods that were refused — it can take ten or more tastes before a toddler's taste buds come around. What tends to backfire is pressure: forcing, bribing with treats, or punishing can actually make a child dislike foods they might otherwise have liked. This is general guidance; if you're worried about your child's growth or nutrition, talk to your pediatrician.

related.title: Starting Solid Foods
related.hook: Most babies are ready for their first solid foods at around six months — alongside continued breast milk or formula, not instead of it.

related.title: Foods to Skip Before Baby's First Birthday
related.hook: A few foods are genuinely risky for babies under one — honey can cause botulism, cow's milk shouldn't be the main drink yet, and round, hard foods are choking hazards.

flashcards.prompt: What is the 'division of responsibility' in feeding a toddler?

choices.text: Parent decides what and when to offer; child decides whether and how much to eat
The child decides what foods are bought and cooked each day
The parent decides exactly how many bites the child must eat

flashcards.explanation_html: Parents handle the menu and timing; children handle their own appetite. This keeps mealtimes calmer and respects a child's hunger and fullness cues.

flashcards.prompt: About how many tastes can it take before a toddler accepts a new food?
flashcards.back_html: As many as 10 or more times tasting it. Keep offering rejected foods calmly, without pressure — exposure over time is what helps.
